479131,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.5.2,1917-07-18,20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0,ca.m.7879,Mr. BOIVIN:,,' DAYLIGHT SAVING.,,,The Daylight Saving Bill has been awaiting its second reading since June 15. I have just received a personal letter from a prominent employee of the Grand Trunk Railway company, part of which reads:

May I also ask if the Government will do anything with the Daylight Saving Bill? If it is brought in for Canada and not for the United States, it will, of course, quite considerably affect train schedules. I would like to be informed thereon as far in advance as possible, as we are quite seriously interested.

May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if it is the intention of the Government to put this Bill through during the present session? If so, in view of the fact that the summer season is quite far advanced, will the proclamation bringing the Act into operation be issued this year, or will it he held over until next season?

,Liberal,,Georges Henri Boivin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=20153f1d-4d12-4d52-b34f-744ffb0e1cd0&Language=E&Section=ALL
479132,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.5.3,1917-07-18,2cf93f16-ac02-4963-ae74-f74b1cb23251,ca.m.6710,Sir GEORGE FOSTER:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,' DAYLIGHT SAVING.,,,That is a matter for the House to decide. I intend to introduce the Bill at the first convenient opportunity and to make a full explanation of it. Undoubtedly a large part of the season has passed during which a daylight saving measure would be useful. In the United States a similar measure has passed through the Senate and will come into operation next year. It may be advisable for us to take up the discussion of the Bill with a view of keeping in line with the course followed by the United States.

RODOLPHE LEMIEUX:,,CIVIL SERVICE INSURANCE.,,,Since the Military Service Bill came before the House I have received several letters from young men who are liable to be called upon for military service, inquiring whether the Government intends to amend the Insurance Act with a' view to fixing a maximum amount of premium, covering war risk, payable on their policies. The insurance companies, as my hon. friend knows, charge a higher premium for war risks. There is a feeling among these young men that when they are called they will be unable to keep up their insurance policies because of the extra premium. I would ask the Prime Minister-I do not see the Minister of Finance in his seat-to consider this- matter. When the Bill is before the House for third reading, I intend to bring the matter up again.

FRANK OLIVER:,,FORBIDDEN CIRCULATION IN CANADA.,,,I have here a book called ""The Fiddlers"" by Arthur Mee. It was sent to me through the mails; I believe that copies have been received by a number of other members of Parliament. As I heard some question about this matter I looked up the Canada Gazette of Saturday, July 14, and on page 104 found the following:
Censorship Notice.
Consolidated Orders Respecting Censorship.
Department of the Secretary of State of Canada,
Ottawa, 11th July, 1917.
Notice is hereby given that, in pursuance of the Consolidated Orders respecting Censor-

ship, dated the 17th day of January, 1917, passed under the provisions of section 6, of the War Measures Act, 1914, a hook entitled ""The Fiddlers,"" by Arthur Mee, published by Morgan & Scott, Limited, 12 Paternoster Buildings, England, has been declared by the Secretary of State of Canada, to contain objectionable matter as defined by the Consolidated Orders respecting Censorship, and that the possession within Canada of any issue or copy of the said ""The Fiddlers,"" whether heretofore or hereafter published, has been prohibited by a ""Warrant of the Secretary of State of Canada, dated the 12th July, 1917, and that, as provided by paragraph 3 (1) of Order 111 of the said Consolidated Orders respecting Censorship, any person guilty of an offence against the said Orders shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars or imprisonment for any term not exceeding five years, or to both such fine and such imprisonment.
Thomas Mulvey, Under-Secretary of State.

,Liberal,,Frank Oliver,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6e8d69a0-c443-4d32-9982-364df1473067&Language=E&Section=ALL

479141,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.7.4,1917-07-18,6e8d69a0-c443-4d32-9982-364df1473067,ca.m.2836,Mr. OLIVER:,,FORBIDDEN CIRCULATION IN CANADA.,,,I have the book and I have read it in part. It is a powerful arraignment of the liquor traffic in the United Kingdom. I have read the order in council of Wednesday, the 17th of January, 1917, consolidating orders respecting censorship, and I desire to ask the Government under what paragraph of these consolidated orders this notice has been issued, and in respect of what portion of the matter contained in this book?

,Liberal,,Frank Oliver,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6e8d69a0-c443-4d32-9982-364df1473067&Language=E&Section=ALL
479142,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.7.5,1917-07-18,5e8a24b4-f155-4f3d-aacc-e6da13c93756,ca.m.4254,Sir ROBERT BORDEN:,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,FORBIDDEN CIRCULATION IN CANADA.,,,I am afraid that I am in the same unfortunate position under the law as my hon. friend, because a copy of the book has also been sent to me. Possibly I may have shifted the responsibility, as I handed over my copy to one of the officers of the department to peruse until I should have an opportunity of doing so myself. The prohibition of the book did not come to my notice until a copy of it was sent to' me, inviting me to peruse it and see whether there was any good reason why it should be prohibited.
I shall make inquiries as to the matter about which my hon. friend asks for information, and let him know the result at a later date.

479148,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.8.1.2,1917-07-18,unmatched,,,,EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.,STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.,,With reference to the resolution for an extension of the parliamentary term, which was under debate yesterday and was voted on last night, hon. gentlemen will have observed that I did not make any motion that the resolution should be sent with a message to the Senate for the purpose of securing concurrent action there. My failure to take that course was due to the reason which I set forth when moving the resolution. I then declared that I did not think it should be acted upon unless there was unanimity or practical unanimity in the House with regard to it. The result of the vote upon the resolution showed something very far short of either unanimity or practical unanimity, for the vote stood 82 in support of the resolution and 62 against. Under the circumstances, therefore, and having regard to the course which I laid down in moving the resolution, I desire to announce what must already be apparent to hon. gentlemen in this House, that the Government do not purpose taking any further action upon the resolution, as it was carried by a majority of only 20.

479152,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.9.1.2,1917-07-18,52a4499f-fa60-4960-92e4-bb99baf0c85e,ca.m.8507,Mr. TURRIFF:,,FARM LABOUR IN WESTERN CANADA.,MOTION BY MR. TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,"I shall detain the House for only a few moments. The securing of farm help is of very great importance to the people of the West. We are now in the middle of July, and usually harvesting begins within two or three weeks of this date. In order to bring the matter quickly before the House, I shall read an article that appears in the Manitoba Free Press of July Ilth, 1917, under the heading, The Farmers' Forum:
Farm Labour Problem.

Every few days letters arrive for this column, commenting on the extreme shortage of labour for harvest and threshing and suggesting methods by which the shortage may be met. The same suggestions appear in varying forms in all the letters received.
These suggestions, stated broadly, are:
First:
column2: Conscript the slackers in cities ana

column1: towns, place them in the army and return to the farms sufficient numbers of farmers and farm labourers to take care of the crop. In other words conscript man power and send it to do the task for which it is best fitted.""
Second:
column2: Conscript alien enemy labour and

column1: compel them to do the farm work at something like reasonable wages; a few suggest that as they would be fed on the farms they should be paid army wages only, others, however, ask merely for a reasonable rate of wages, and some security that these men when hired will live up to their contract.""

The object of this editorial is not to discuss either of these proposals, but rather to discuss the methods which are being adopted to secure help, more especially with reference to Manitoba; also the outlook for help for all three provinces.

First, as to what has been done. Louis Kon, the head of the immigration department for Manitoba, who has this matter in charge, as soon as the spring rush was over began to lay plans for harvest. With a view to ascertaining the requirements of the farmers, he circularized the secretary of every municipality in Manitoba, suggesting that the council appoint one or more reliable men in each municipality, who would act as agents for the free distribution of labour, who would ascertain the needs of the municipality and transmit them to the immigration office, and who could be applied to to look after the menr when they are ready to go out and see that they reach their proper destinations. . The* ready and general response to this suggestion is an excellent indication of the feeling in the country that help will be short and that there will be difficulty in securing it. It may be assumed that there will be on record in the immigration office, in the course of the next three weeks, a ' very complete list of the requirements of the province.
A careful review has been made of the source of possible supply, and frankly the outlook is not encouraging.
The sources, roughly, are:
column2: Homesteaders

column1: within the province, a limited supply of agricultural college student labour from the United States and possibly a percentage of regular farm labour from those States with crops which mature at an earlier date than our own.

A certain percentage of the labour employed in large establishments in the cities and towns, which volunteered last spring, and when not called upon for spring work, was asked to hold itself in reserve for the greater needs of harvest.
A possible percentage from the province of Quebec, the large alien population in the west available only at very high wages.

With regard to homesteaders, many of whom are aliens, it must be remembered that while a large number of them were available last spring, there will not be so many this harvest for the simple reason that last spring these men doubled up, and one man put in the crop of four or five while they went to help with the seeding elsewhere. In harvest it will take from four to five men to take off what one man seeded, and it is just as important that their crops be saved in good order as any other.
Student labour from the United States will be highly efficient, but it is not yet sure that

it will be available in any large numbers as it may be needed at home. If any large number can be secured these young men will work in groups, moving from point to point as they are needed, and will, no doubt, be of great value, as they will work with trained brains as well as trained hands.

Regular farm labour from the United States is a very uncertain quantity at present. It will not be available from the States immediately to the south, the Dakotas and Minnesota, as their crop is almost as late as our own. There is a possibility, however, some may be secured from the winter wheat states. The provincial immigration office is in communication with Assistant Secretary Vrooman, of the Department of Agriculture, Washington, seeing what it may be possible to do along this line.

With regard to help from industrial concerns and large city establishments, many or these are already working with a very short staff, so that the number from this source cannot be large. It may be found necessary to close all the industrial concerns for a few weeks, with the exception of the munition works and industries manufacturing foods either for home consumption or shipment overseas, and send every available man and every ablebodied woman employed in these industries to the country.

Help from Quebec is highly problematic, unless it is conscripted for the purpose. Already signs are not wanting that Quebec is preparing to refuse work in western harvest fields in retaliation for western members of Parliament voting for the Conscription Bill. The alien labour at home is equally problematic until it is definitely known whether or not these men are to be conscripted, if the Bill goes through. Nothing short of compulsion will make many of them work at all, or any of them work for less than the very highest wages which necessity may drive-farmers to pay. At least this is the information furnished by very many farmers and farmers' organizations.

From interviews in the papers, on the return of Sir George Foster from Washington, it appeared as if he had made arrangements with regard to help from the United States, but upon inquiry it is learned that nothing but generalities were discussed and no plans laid by the federal minister.

Inquiry also reveals the fact that nothing is being done or planned along this line by the head of the National Service Commission. It would have been reasonable to expect that the information gathered from the National Service cards would have been available for the purpose of ascertaining the various classes of labour available, but up to date so far as the public have any knowledge this has not been tabulated. The indications are that so far as farm labour is concerned each province is to be allowed to shift for itself.

This is not as it should be. The shortage of labour is so very great that the only way of meeting the difficulty is to have available supplies mobilized and moved from point to point as needed. This can only be effectively accomplished by federal authorities. They too are the only people in a position to deal with the matter of transportation. Labour should be carried at the very lowest rate from point to point and with the minimum of red tape about securing this transportation. Last spring low rates could only be secured for

groups ot five or over, from points outside of Winnipeg, whereas they should be equally available for one man if that one man is all that is needed at a given point. Moreover, transportation should be useable on any train, passenger or freight.

The foregoing gives some idea of the gravity of the labour situation. It is not a matter of securing help for the farmers in order that they may make a profit out of their crop; it is something vastly more important. It is the need of securing help for the farmers to save the crop, in order that our men, fighting in the trenches, may be properly supplied with food that we may have sufficient for our own tables and also that we supply as far as possible the needs of Britain for bread. Everything from Britain indicates that rationing is steadily becoming tighter.

The crop of every homesteader, who may have in no more than 20 or 30 acres, has suddenly become of national and indeed of Empire-wide importance. The west, in times of peace, claimed boastfully that she was the bread basket of the Empire. Now is the time to make good that boasting.

The article I have read deals with the matter so fully that I do not think it is necessary for me to add anything further than to say that this is a very very serious question. TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend (Mr. Turiff) has brought this matter to the attention of the House, as it is appropriate that the steps which have been taken by the Government with regard thereto should be known. The subject has been more immediately under the attention of my colleague the Minister of the Interior who will give, on certain ^aspects of the question, more detailed information than I can offer at the moment.

I may, however, say that negotiations have been going on for some time between the Government of Canada, through our Department of the Interior, and the Government of the United States, through one of its departments, for co-operation in the supply of labour, so that what is not required in one country may at a particular time of need in another country be used as far as is reasonably possible in the last-named country. As a result of negotiations between the officers of the Department of the Interior and officers of the United States Government a memorandum to carry out this purpose was drawn up, which was submitted to the Government of Canada and approved immediately. It has also been approved by the Government of the United States, and it will come into operation at once. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior will explain it more fully.

So far as other steps are concerned, there was a meeting called last week, at my instance, which was attended by representatives of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand 'Trunk railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway. I also asked ithe attendance of a representative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, a representative of the Canadian Bankers' Association, and representatives of the Imperial Munitions Board. The meeting was held on Saturday last.

The object of asking representatives of the Bankers' Association., the Manufacturers' Association and the Imperial Munitions Board, was to ascertain whether or not some means could he contrived by which, during the brief period of the harvest, when labour is so urgently necessary, some men might be spared from the activities of those carrying on. industries and banking, and it was thought also that the Imperial Munitions Board could oo-operate to some extent. The meeting was also attended by Mr. Peterson, secretary of the National Service Board. While the article to which my hon. friend has called the attention of the House is very instructive and useful, I think the writer was under a misapprehension, in one respect. The returns, received 'by the National Service Board have been tabulated and Mr. Peterson informs us that there are 250,000 people, or thereabouts, in Canada, who, in returning their cards, stated that they would be willing to go to some other part of the country upon the condition that their remuneration should not be less than they were then receiving and that their transportation expenses should be paid. Of course, I do not mean

to suggest that anything like 250,000 people would be available for this purpose, but it would seem to indicate that the information obtained by the National Service Board in that regard might be of use. There was a very hopeful feeling as to the provision of necessary labour expressed at this meeting and especially by the representatives of the railway companies who have had such questions before them year [DOT]after year, and who say that the grave apprehensions entertained from time to time have not- been realized. They 'believe that sufficient labour will be provided this year.

The meeting was also attended by several of the ministers whose departments appertain especially to this matter. When we had completed the conference of an hour, the representatives of the railways, of the associations to which I have alluded and of the Imperial Munitions Board and the National Service Board, spent some further time in devising the best means of co-operation. They have embodied their conclusions in a memorandum setting forth the lines along which they purpose to act, and included in the course which they intend to take is an effort by the secretary of the National Service Board to get in touch with the persons who have indicated their willingness to transfer their labour to other parts of the country, especially such as are not engaged in industries that are vitally essential to the carrying on of the war. It is not intended to apply to those whose skill in a particular industry or service would be of more advantage than in any other occupation. That, briefly stated, is the situation as I understand it at present. We are keeping .in touch with the railway companies and the boards and associations represented at the meeting. It was in pursuance of a suggestion made at this meeting that I placed the situation before the people of Canada generally, and asked for their good will and co-operation in order that the harvest now ripening may be gathered and that there may be no loss to the country by any failure so to. gather it.

479154,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.9.1.4,1917-07-18,56470474-43c7-4392-9d18-c5e1c4bcdfef,ca.m.5902,Mr. BUCHANAN:,,FARM LABOUR IN WESTERN CANADA.,MOTION BY MR. TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,I am quite sure that the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) will be encouraging to the farmers of the West, who have been in doubt as to the supply of farm labour. I am not going to speak of the West as a whole, but I wish to make a few remarks about the obstacles which face the farmers of the southern part of Alberta. As the House knows, there was a coal strike in the spring and many miners were available for

farm work. Now that the mines have resumed operations, and will, we hope, be busily engaged for the rest of the year, there is no possibility of any labour from that source being available for farm work. We have been accustomed to get some labour from the United States, and this w.as particularly so last year. Our harvest is coming on almost at the moment that the United States is calling men up under the selective draft, and there is no doubt that the supplies from that source will be depleted. In the southern part of Alberta the acreage under crop is 10 per cent greater than it was last year, and consequently the demand for help will be heavy. Some effort should be made to organize farm labour for the harvest, and to this end the co-operation of, the .provincial governments should be secured. If it is possible to transfer men from one section of Canada to the other in order to carry on farm work that system should be adopted. In some parts of the country the harvest will be earlier than in others, and the men might be shifted from one place to another. If such a system were adopted it would be of considerable assistance. In the past the men have gone to one district, remained there until the work was concluded and then they have drifted away, but frequently not to the places where there was a demand for their labour. By the proper organization of the men that situation would be relieved. I appreciate what the Government is doing to meet the situation. The chief trouble at present is that farmers are afraid that they will not have any labour, and if they could get an assurance that there is the possibility that labour will be provided as it is needed it would help to relieve their apprehension on this score.

,Liberal,,William Ashbury Buchanan,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56470474-43c7-4392-9d18-c5e1c4bcdfef&Language=E&Section=ALL
479155,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.9.1.5,1917-07-18,896b827c-c49c-4978-9b77-7590d414c5ee,ca.m.7312,Mr. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior,FARM LABOUR IN WESTERN CANADA.,MOTION BY MR. TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has already pretty well covered the arrangements which have been undertaken by the Government in order to secure the necessary farm help. But possibly I might elaborate a little the arrangement that has been made between the United States and Canada. When my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was in Washington he took the matter up informally with representatives of the United States Government. We sent down the Deputy Minister of the Interior and the Inspector of Immigration agencies in the United States to consult with the authorities at Washington. They had an interview with representatives

of the labour, agriculture and immigration departments of the United States and a tentative arrangements was made to be submitted to the respective governments for their approval. Pending its consummation, an official was to be appointed by both Governments to carry out the operations under the arrangement.Thearrangement is, in short:-

column2: That the Canadian Department of the Interior will place no obstacles in the way of the entry of the United States across the Canada-New England boundary of agricultural and lumbering labourers, not needed at the particular time in the lumber and agricultural industries of Canada, to take part in the harvesting of the potato and other crops in New England and elsewhere, and in the cutting and rafting of timber in the New England woods, as hereinafter mentioned, or in the way of the entry into the United States across the boundary between Canada and the States of Minnesota, North Dakota and Montana, of farm labourers to participate in the harvesting of wheat in the States mentioned; hut, on the contrary, the said Department will, through its immigration officials and in all other ways open to it, encourage the coming of such surplus agricultural and lumbering help into the portions of the United States specified, and in pursuance of that policy will endeavour to have conveyed to Western Canada, sufficiently in advance of the opening of the harvest season there, such harvest helpers as may hereafter be reported to them by the United States Department of Labour to be needed in the States of Minnesota, North and South Dakota and Montana and other States, so that such helpers may promply cross the line and assist the forces mobilized by the United States Government in the harvest fields of the said States.

That the United States Departments of Labour and Agriculture will not only permit but encourage such surplus agricultural labourers among those now mobilized for harvesting purposes in the middle West, as rapidly as the need for them in the harvest fields of the United States decreases or disappears, to cross the boundary into the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan and there assist in the harvesting of the wheat crop, and that appropriate instructions will be given all immigration and other officials of the United States looking to the end that the surplus supply of farm labour in the middle western portion of the United States may be made available to western Canada in the manner and for the purpose stated.

That Canada and the United States will mutually enforce, through their Immigration Services or otherwise, such precautionary measures as may be needed to insure that all persons whose departure from the respective countries is permitted will be required to return to the country of origin immediately that the temporary purpose involved in their admission to the other country has been accomplished.

That as soon as this tentative agreement is approved by the appropriate officials of the respective Governments an officer or officers will be selected by each Government to devise and execute the details of a plan of operation.

column1: This has been approved by the Canadian Government, and we have information that it has been approved by the American Gov-

emment, and. the officials herein mentioned will be appointed to carry out the arrangement. I quite agree that there is a great shortage of farm labour in the West. At the same time, we have had the same cry for many years past on behalf of the Provincial Governments and of the farmers, and I can say without exaggeration that usually they d.o not err on the -side of -asking for less than they reailly require. On the contrary, I think that their needs, have been supplied by considerably less numbers than the estimates of the respective Provincial Governments. For instance, this spring an arrangement was made between the Provincial Governments -and the Dominion that certain immigration officials were to be -sent to the United States by the provincial -authorities to act in co-operation with Dominion officers in securing farm help to put in the crops. The Provincial Governments estimated a much larger number than they required. By reaispn of a very active publicity campaign in the United States, we were able to secure several thousand additional helpers from the United States, sufficient to supply the demands. Owing, ho-wever, to the United States sin-ce then coming into the war, we could not, of course, in justice to that country, inaugurate a -similar campaign for harvesters, and therefore the arrangement I have just read has been made on the h-asis of co-operation -between the respective Governments to help fill the requirements p-f the farmers and others in the respective countries. Last year it. w-as estimated that we would require from 35,000 to 40,000 harvesters in the -three provinces of the West. There were sent in toy the transportation companies from the East, in round numbers, 27,000 men. About 4,000 of those came from the United States. Som-ewfaere in th-e neighborhood of 3,000 entered through th-e western ports and nearly 2,000 through the eastern ports. The transportation companies allowed a special rate of $10 to Winnipeg and the men were distributed to the various portions of the three provinces at a rate of half a cent a mile. There was a return rate of, I think, $18. I have asked the transportation eo-mpanie-s to grant an even lower rate if possible for the ensuing season, and, while they have not committed themselves, they ar-e considering it, and I hope that a cheap rate may be secured.

The article read contains some very practical suggestions, of which some have already been acted upon, while others I think will be rather impracticable. For instance, the suggestion is made that we should conscript the alien enemies and the

slackers and compel them to work at a fixed maximum wage. An effort was made to do this in connection with spring work in Manitoba, and I understand that there was a proposition from the Grain Growers to the Provincial Government to fix a maximum wage, so that each farmer could secure help at a reasonable wage. The Provincial Government, however, could not see their way clear to accede to that request. You may take a horse to water but you cannot compel him to drink; and while you can conscript men to fight in defence of their country, while they will fight because they are fighting in defence of their own lives in the trenches, it is another thing to compel men to go into the harvest field and work there. I am afraid that if we compelled men-to work in that way the farmer who employed such men would obtain very little result from their labour. The Prime Minister has already said that a conference was held here a few days ago between the various bodies he mentioned. We are going to leave no stone unturned in order to secure the necessary help. All of these bodies have promised to use their influence in their respective spheres to release as many men, under their jurisdiction as they possibly can, in order to provide the necessary amount of help. The Deputy Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan visited Ottawa and had an interview with me last week, and we have promised co-operation, so far as possible, with his Government. The Provincial Government are willing to distribute any help that goes into that province. They are also carrying on a propaganda locally to secure men. Last year there were ticketed out from towns and cities in Saskatchewan, 3,700 men for farm work. In Alberta there were ticketed out from cities and towns 3,200, and from Winnipeg about 5,000, so that the local supply was quite large. However, we do realize that there were a number of soldiers in Canada last year. There were some 16,000 in Camp Hughes and some 3,000 at Sarcee Camp, who were released, nominally to help on the farms. I do not say that all went to. farm work, in fact I ""know that many did not. But owing to the fact that there are comparatively few troops in Canada to-day, we cannot draw on this source as we did last year. Every possible thing that can be done will be aone by this department in the interest of the farmers, in co-operation with the Pro-223i
vincial Governments and those other bodies that have been mentioned.

479160,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.9.1.10,1917-07-18,3c716a03-43b1-401d-820f-7921b10e5565,ca.m.6937,Mr. ROBB:,,FARM LABOUR IN WESTERN CANADA.,MOTION BY MR. TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,The shortage of labour anticipated in western Canada is now on in eastern Canada. In support of his argument for labour to reap the crops of western Canada, the hon.. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) quoted an article in the Winnipeg Free Press. One feature of that article struck me, that was the statement that the people of Quebec were refusing to work in the western wheat fields as retaliation for the"" imposition of military service. That is only in. line with a lot of other misrepresentation of the province of Quebec that have been spoiling paper and ink for the last few weeks throughout this country. All throughout eastern Canada to-day, while the haying is on, as every hon. gentleman from Ontario and Quebec knows, labour is almost unobtainable. Farmers are now offering $3 to $5 a day for help and are unable to obtain it, and you will find women working in the hayfields of eastern Canada. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has said that western Canada is the bread basket of the Empire, and perhaps this is true. But I hope that our friends in the West will not forget that eastern Canada provides the cheese and the butter to put on that bread. And providing cheese and butteT does not mean work for three or four weeks in the .springtime, and three or four weeks during

the gathering of harvest; it means hard and slavish work every day of the year, and many farmers of eastern Canada have lessened their herds because they were unable to obtain labour to take eare of them. While it is important to have labour to put in and gather the crops, it is equally important to have labour to move that crop to market. Last year, in western Canada, they raised a pretty fair crop of grain that would have been useful for the feeding of cattle in eastern Canada, but, owing to the shortage of labour to operate the railways, to get out coal or supply fuel for the engines, that *crop was allowed to remain during the winter, and they were unable to move it until the grass was growing in eastern Canada, *and it was not required. The result of the shortage of labour wasi that throughout eastern Canada the canners of this country were buying cattle at reduced prices, because the farmers had no feed for their cattle. I say it is equally as important that the Government should provide labour for the coal mines, and labour to operate the railways of this country to move the crops as it is that they shall provide labour to gather the crops. We heard a good deal of complaint about Canada not being able to produce potatoes for the requirements of her people last year, but many people know that there were thousands of bushels of potatoes left on the railway sidings in Montreal, because there was no labour to move them until the frost came along and spoiled them. Those are the conditions we are faced with, and I think the Government should take these matters into account when considering the labour question. While the labour conditions may be acute in the western country, it is more so in eastern Canada. Industries are nearly closing down or they are running shorthanded because there is no labour, and it is a libel upon the province of Quebec to say that labourers refused to work on account of the conscription measure. Labourers in Quebec are ready to work wherever they can get a day's pay, and there are more men wanting to help than there is labour offering.

TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,I desire to call the attention of the Government to a matter which came to my notice last fall. The Minister of the Interior speaks about labour sent out from Camp Hughes. That labour was very useful in our part of the country, but it had a very disturbing influence in another way. A great many of us who were running threshing outfits

were dependent on some of those recruits for helping to run the threshing outfit, and in the middle of the threshing season they were taken off, and the work was not completed. The result was the work dragged along, and practically no fall ploughing was done at all, and we have much less wheat in crop this year than in other years. I know it from experience. I have had men taken away from me, and I know how it works.

TURRIFF IN REFERENCE THERETO.,,I may say that every year in Ontario we suffer a great deal in the fall of the year from the advertisements for labour for the West. They take our men away from us in the fall of the year, when we require them very badly, and I was going to suggest to my hon. friend that, in his organization, he should look after the taking of labour from one place to the other more by organization than by wild advertisements as to high prices and that sort of thing, because that has a tendency to make men restless and make them leave their work. If a man has two or three .men employed, or perhaps only one man, we know they simply leave when they like. Very frequently you dare not say anything to them. They get up and leave you, and that is caused a great deal by advertisements which appear in the fall of the year for labour in the West. My hon. friend who preceded me spoke of the necessity for labour for various industries and for transportation. He is absolutely right, and labour in our section of Ontario is just as scarce as it is anywhere else. I quite appreciate that it is necessary to move the harvest in the West, but it is also necessary to move our crops in the East.

479187,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.2,1917-07-18,8c3f1b44-33c3-456b-92a4-2d9ab84b0e8c,ca.m.7822,Mr. HERMENEGILDE BOULAY (translation!) :,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,"Mr. Chairman, allow me to

call your attention to subsection 2 of section 302 which is of very great importance to the travelling public, in the province of Quebec. Monday last, when we were in committee on the Bill, I stated that it would be proper to amend this subsection, so as to make it more satisfactory to the travelling public in my province. The proposed amendment would affect exclusively the province of Quebec and I fail to see that it could cause any inconvenience in the other parts of Canada. I hope the suggestion will be considered to be in the best interest of the public. I do not expect that any member from the province of Quebec will oppose the amendment; I rather believe that it will meet the views of all. '

The amendment that I suggest affects only the province of Quebec. Members from that province know the inconvenience that has been' suffered in the past by the travelling public in that section of the country by

reason of the fact 'that a great many of the conductors, brakemen, baggage masters, station agents and ticket agents cannot understand the language of persons boarding and leaving trains. This amendment would effect a great improvement over present conditions. Several times I have acted as interpreter on behalf of persons who were travelling, because railway employees were nnable to understand them. Every company moving trains in the province of Quebec should require its employees to understand both languages. They wouild have no difficulty in selecting from amongst their own employees persons who could speak both languages. Subsection 2 of this section reads:
Every railway company shall print in both the English and French languages the time tables that are to be used along its lines within the limits of the province of Quebec.
I move that this subsection be amended by adding thereto the following words:
And all employees coming in contact with the travelling public shall understand both official languages of the country.

ARMSTRONG:,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) has moved an amendment to clause 302 to the effect that both languages shall be spoken by the crews on the railroads running through the province of Quebec.

479192,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.7,1917-07-18,22bac231-c23b-4794-8dfb-46bf52cd7616,ca.m.9821,Mr. PAQUET (translation):,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,Mr. Chairman, I approve entirely of the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay). I have myself witnessed of late unfortunate occurrences due to the fact that the railway employees could not understand what the passengers meant. Now the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has just made a statement; but I think we could request the hon Minister of Railways and Canals to do his best to have that amendment inserted in the Act, for the greater 'convenience of the travelling public in the province of Quebec.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Eugène Paquet,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=22bac231-c23b-4794-8dfb-46bf52cd7616&Language=E&Section=ALL
479193,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.8,1917-07-18,8c3f1b44-33c3-456b-92a4-2d9ab84b0e8c,ca.m.7822,Mr. BOULAY (translation):,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,,Conservative (1867-1942),,Herménégilde Boulay,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8c3f1b44-33c3-456b-92a4-2d9ab84b0e8c&Language=E&Section=ALL
479194,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.9,1917-07-18,8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a,ca.m.1140,Mr. MARCIL:,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,To appreciate this question properly, our friends from Ontario should think for a moment of the condition passengers w.ould be in if a Frenchman who could not understand English was in charge of a train running through Ontario. That would not be in the interests of the passengers or of the country. In the province of Quebec, although a large number of our people speak the English language, unfortunately a great many do not, especially those' from the rural parts of the province, and the district of Quebec in particular. The result is that a conductor in charge of a train may have a car full of people with whom he is unable to communicate. Having regard to the fact

that railroad companies operating in the province of Quebec .already print their time tables, hills of lading, posters, and so on _ in both languages to facilitate the transaction of business, I see no reason why the train crews should not 'be required to speak both French and English. It is very awkward for people who are stranded at a railway station and are unable to make themselves understood.

,Liberal,,Charles Marcil,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a&Language=E&Section=ALL
479195,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.10,1917-07-18,fec8fb76-539a-4343-9bea-79ced68f163b,ca.m.6654,Mr. NESBITT:,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,Do not nearly all the
railway men understaand French?

,Liberal,,Edward Walter Nesbitt,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=fec8fb76-539a-4343-9bea-79ced68f163b&Language=E&Section=ALL
479196,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.11,1917-07-18,8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a,ca.m.1140,Mr. MABOIL:,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,'The ticket sellers, of

course, are .able to speak both languages, and the conductors as well; that is elementary. I do not want to be harsh; a certain length of time should be allowed the railway companies in which to make this change. My experience is that a large number of the old conductors who have been employed on the roads in the province of Quebec for (the last thirty or forty years can speak both languages, but men are being brought in more and more from western Canada who are unable to speak French, .and that is a great inconvenience to the travelling public and the public generally.

If the matter were property placed before the Canadian labour unions and if they understood it, I certainly think thej would not object to the encouragement of the learning of both languages, especially in the province of Quebec, because it is evident that it is to a man's own interest if he wants to do any business that he should be able to speak both languages. I think it should be encouraged on the railways, because after all the railways deal with the public. The Minister of Railways might give the companies fair warning that m a year or a year and a half the ticket seller and the conductor at least-those who come in direct contact with the public- should understand the two languages.

,Liberal,,Charles Marcil,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a&Language=E&Section=ALL
479197,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.13.12,1917-07-18,d0ceec5f-f083-4ad4-8139-eadbb88a7dcf,ca.m.8966,Mr. PROULX:,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.,,,I am strongly in favour
of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay).

Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG; I do not want it understood that I am opposed to the crews being able to speak the French language. I should think it would he a very great advantage if they could do so. I merely called the attention of the committee to the position in which the railroads are placed at the present time, especially on the main lines in and out of important cities in Quebec. To pass this amendment would be to say that nobody but French Canadians should be employed

,Liberal,,Edmond Proulx,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d0ceec5f-f083-4ad4-8139-eadbb88a7dcf&Language=E&Section=ALL

479199,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.14.1.1,1917-07-18,,,,stagedirection,,,,on railroads in the province of Quebec. The result would, be that the railway unions, [DOT] the large majority of whose membership are English-speaking, would be sure to retaliate and prevent French Canadians from being employed outside the province of Quebec.

Mr. MARCH,: There are a large number of English-speaking Canadians in the province of Quebec who can speak both languages. It is a great mistake to imagine that only the French Canadians speak both languages.

479200,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.14.2,1917-07-18,9b9087eb-6add-462b-bc28-48898b45eb69,ca.m.4640,Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG:,,S514 COMMONS,,,"I am quite well aware of that fact. What I called the attention of the committee to is the fact that the representatives of the railway unions are strongly opposed to an amendment of this nature being placed in the Bill.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Joseph Elijah Armstrong,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9b9087eb-6add-462b-bc28-48898b45eb69&Language=E&Section=ALL
479201,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.14.3,1917-07-18,82d7e9e4-2cdc-418e-94b5-1b115c88ac94,ca.m.1846,Mr. WRIGHT:,,S514 COMMONS,,,When the matter was up before I suggested that it might very well be left in the hands of the Railway Commission, and if they had not the power to deal with it, such power might be conferred upon them. We can very well see it might be a great hardship to put a clause of this kind in as an ironclad rule. Take, for instance, a train leaving Halifax for Vancouver; because it ran through a portion of Quebec for an hour or two, would it be right to compel the crew to be able to speak the French language? Might it not be a very great hardship indeed, and interfere with the running arrangements of such trains? On the local trains running between cities in Quebec it would be no great hardship to a railway if it had to have men who could speak both French and English, and I can understand that such an order might very well be made. At the same time I think it should be left in the hands of the Railway Commission.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,William Wright,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82d7e9e4-2cdc-418e-94b5-1b115c88ac94&Language=E&Section=ALL
479202,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.14.4,1917-07-18,733cae8a-7e57-46c6-ab2e-478ac991835f,ca.m.4942,Mr. LEMIEUX:,,S514 COMMONS,,,I wish to thank my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) for the very sensible remarks he has made, and I think it would be well if my hon. friend from Rimouski were to accept his suggestion. If a provision were placed in the Act whereby the Railway Commission might regulate this matter, we would come to a satisfactory conclusion, because the province of Quebec is represented on the commission and I am sure the interests of the province would be well looked after.

I may assure the committee this question is not brought forward with the idea of raising a vexed question. There is a real grievance in some cases. I quite agree with my hon. friend that we cannot expect a bilingual crew on a train leaving Halifax

or St. John for Vancouver, yet one must recollect that on a long-haul train partial changes of crews are made. A conductor might take the train from Halifax to Montreal, and be relieved there, so it would simply be a matter of arrangement. It might be arranged that when a train reaches the boundary line between New Brunswick and Quebec a conductor speaking both languages would be put in charge. Certain grievances on this subject have been made public. Two cases were given a little more publicity than the others. One concerned some young boys coming home from college, and the other was a case of gross misconduct on the part of a conductor on the Canadian Northern Railway. In the first instance, some students were going from Rigaud to Montreal. They were threatened with arrest by the conductor of the train because they could not understand him, and he insisted that they should understand him. The doors of the car were locked, and had it not been for the intervention of a gentleman whose name was mentioned, those boys would have been arrested when they reached Montreal, because, according to the conductor, they had refused to pay their fares. The case which happened on the Canadian Northern was on a new line in a new district. The conductor was ignorant of the language of the passengers, and on the occasion referred to he handled very roughly one of the passengers who did not understand him. When the remonstrance was made to the company in Toronto they took the matter up and the answer was very satisfactory. Apologies were made, and the company promised that such conduct would not be renewed. These are only two instances which occur to my mind at the present time as tending to show there certainly are grievances.

But as the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) stated, the local conditions could be looked after if the power was given to .the Railway Board to deal with such conditions. I would be agreeable to accepting that suggestion, and I would suggest to my hon. friend from Rimouski that he amend his motion accordingly. It is well that this grievance be met before the committee, because certainly there has been some wild talk of late about it on the various trains.

,Liberal,,Rodolphe Lemieux,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=733cae8a-7e57-46c6-ab2e-478ac991835f&Language=E&Section=ALL
479203,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.14.5,1917-07-18,93ee7742-7392-4af4-8f6f-57873f62985f,ca.m.2267,Mr. GREEN:,,S514 COMMONS,,,I am not in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay), nor am I in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright). This is a matter that should be left as it is. I

see no reason for making it the law that the people in charge of the trains should speak both languages. I quite agree that it would be an advantage, and that it is just and right that where necessary the train officials should speak both languages. freight can be delivered front*-Montreal to the Soo much cheaper by water than by rail, and if the railways are to do business at all they must be allowed to file a tariff to meet the water rate. I have often wondered why that was allowed. I know that the business with which I was connected in my own province some years ago, a foundry and machine shop, was practically driven out of business through our competitors in the lower part of the province being able to send their products to Edmuudston very much cheaper than we could send ours to points a hundred miles nearer. We were not -at a competitive point, and had to pay a local freight rate to get cur goods in, and another local freight rate to get them out. Our competitors could get their freight to the distributing point at Edmundston very much cheaper than we could, alhough it had to be hauled twice as far. That has been going on ever since I was a boy, and I presume that unless somebody like the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) raises a big row about it-and I think if he took this matter up he might achieve some results-the same condition will continue. It does not seem to me to be right; I think there should be some levelling up of the rates. I do not see any reason for taking up the certificate merely because some other conductor is coming on; the fact that you produce your certificate to one conductor should be sufficient. Sometimes the pullman car conductor claims that he is obliged to satisfy the conductor of the train that my certificate is all right and that therefore it is necessary for him to take it. I have some sympathy with the case brought up by the hon. member for Daupbin (Mr. Cruise). These two clauses are read together, as was stated by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong). The first clause of the section gives a definition of a company. It says:

column2: In this section,-

company"" means any person or company having legislative authority from the Parliament of Canada to acquire, construct, operate or maintain works, machinery, plant, lines, poles, tunnels, conduits, or other means for receiving, generating, storing, transmitting, distributing or supplying electricity or other power or energy, but does not include a railway company, or a telegraph company or telephone company.

column1: That is it simply refers to electric light and power companies. It separates telephone and telegraph companies from the others, and cuts it down to dealing expressly with electric light and power companies.

I have no hesitation in saying it is the grossest piece of class or local legislation I have ever heard proposed, much less enacted in law, since I came to this Parliament thirteen or fourteen years ago. The Railway Committee in Parliament has for a great many years been trying to carry out the general provision, which says that nothing shall be done in any municipality without the consent of the municipality, and if the parties interested cannot agree they appeal to the Railway Board, and the decision of the Railway Board is final.

That is the only fair and decent way I can imagine of settling these matters. Some difference arose between the city of Toronto and the Toronto Electric Railway Company. There is the Toronto Electric Light, Heat and Power Company, which is closely bound up with the Toronto Electric Railway Company and also with the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, which, I may say, is the father of them all. The explanation given to the committee was that the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission had spend about five million dollars in the city of Toronto developing the light, heat and power situation, or the city of Toronto, acting under the Hydro Electric Commission, had expended that amount of money. In any event that much money had been spent, and because- they had dealt entirely with the Hydro Electric Commission, they ought to be placed in a position different from any other company or any other corporation or municipality in Canada.

479360,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.15.82,1917-07-18,bd9df755-dfce-42dc-9ebb-55306d610edc,ca.m.3200,Mr. COCHRANE:,Minister of Railways and Canals,P520 COMMONS,,,The policy is that the municipality should control its own streets.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Francis Cochrane,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bd9df755-dfce-42dc-9ebb-55306d610edc&Language=E&Section=ALL
479361,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.15.83,1917-07-18,80f4de9d-1b1a-4db1-93cf-9cb7b9b63dd4,ca.m.9843,Mr. CARVELL:,,P520 COMMONS,,,But that is not the policy in any other place in Canada, and I challenge the minister to put his finger on a solitary statute where any municipality has the right to control its own streets unless it is subject to an appeal to the Railway Board. I know they will tell you this case stands out by itself, but that does not alter the fact that this company got powers from this Parliament, and started operation in good faith. They spent millions and millions of dollars, and now, because the Hydro-Electric Commission, or the people of Toronto acting under the Hydro-Electric Commission spent about five million dollars, they ought to have the right to say the Toronto Electric Light, Company cannot extend their plant or works unless the municipality gives them permission. The municipality told us in so many words they would not give that permission, because they did not want them as competitors, and the sub-committee of this House introduced clause 5 into this Bill simply to give the municipality of Toronto the absolute right to prevent this company from doing business. I protested against it then, and I protest now. I do not suppose my protest will have much weight, but I could not allow class legislation of that character to go through without objection. You may say the city of Toronto ought to have the right

to control their own streets. If my hon. friend will take that attitude with every corporation and every municipality in Canada we will discuss it. If he will say there is no appeal of a municipality to the Railway Board, it is debatable, but to say there is an appeal except in the case of Toronto, to prevent a company which has been doing business there for eighteen years from continuing business, I say is class legislation and should not be allowed. The real cause of the trouble is in the definition given in subsection 1, and the amendment in subsection 5. This is so cunningly worded that unless one had been 'before the sub-committee and had listened to the arguments of the lawyers on both sides one could not tell what it meant. You could not take that section before any court in Canada to-day and get an intelligent interpretation of it unless you had some outside evidence to buttress it up and show what it means. Let me read it:-

(5) The provisions of the last preceding subsection shall apply to and restrict the powers of any company heretofore incorporated by Special Act or other authority of the Parliament of Canada notwithstanding that such provisions may be inconsistent with the provisions of such Special Act or other authority, and notwithstanding the provisions of section three of this Act; and it is hereby declared that the powers of any such company have been so restricted since the date of the enactment of chapter thirty-seven of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1906, that is to say, the thirty-first day of January, 1907.

Carvell) and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and I voted against this clause in committee. I am still of the same opinion. I am especially opposed to that part of the section which . has a retroactive effect. I agree with the minister that a city ought to have control of its own streets. But when we go back for ten years for the purpose of. taking away from a company right, which they acquired in a proper and legal way from this Parliament, and which they have exercised ever since, I think we do something for which there is no justification. Their title to the rights which they claim was sustained by the highest court in the Empire, the Privy Council. We are undertaking in the latter part of this section to take away and nullify the rights that were given the Toronto and Niagara Power Company under a decision of the Privy Council. That is confiscation. While I agree with the minister that in the future the city ought to have the right to control its own streets, and while I would vote for that, I

do not agree with him that we ought to put this retroactive clause in because it would mean taking away a right that was given to this company by an Act of Parliament, and a right which has been sustained by the decision of the highest court in the realm. There is no doubt that it is confiscation. A letter explaining the position was written to the chairman of this committee which I do not think has yet been placed on Hansard. It is as follows:
National Trust Company, Limited,
Toronto, May 26, 1917i Joseph E. Armstrong, Esq., M.P.,
Chairman of Committee sitting on Revision of Railway Act,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-

We are trustees under a bond mortgage dated March 1, 1903, securing an issue of bonds of The Electrical Development Company of Ontario, Limited, maturing in 1933. The total amount of this issue now outstanding is $9,669,500, and of this amount approximately $2,500,000 were issued directly to the British public, and an additional $5,014,000 is held by the British. Empire Trust Company, Limited, of London, England, as security for the debenture stock of the Toronto Power Company, Limited, which debenture stock was issued to the British public. The practical situation, therefore, is that the loss which would be occasioned by any impairment of the security for the bonds of The Electrical Development Company of Ontario, Limited, would primarily fall upon British investors.

As trustees under the said bond mortgage, we hold here as part of the mortgaged premises the whole of the $1,500,000 of bonds and practically all of the capital stock of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. By reason of these holdings, the bondholders of the Electrical Development Company are entitled, as one of the most important parts of their security, not only to the benefit of the physical assets of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company represented by its present and future transmission and distribution lines and other properties but also to the benefit of all its franchises, rights and corporate powers.

The Toronto and Niagara Power Company is a Dominion company incorporated by Chapter 107 of the Statutes of Canada, 2 Edward VII (1902). We are advised that under its Act of Incorporation'the Toronto and Niagara Power Company has, amongst other rights:

column2: The right to supply hydraulic, electric or other power by means of cables, machinery or other appliances;
The right to acquire, construct, maintain and operate works for the production, sale and distribution of electricity and power for any purpose for which such electricity or power can be used ;

The right to construct, maintain and operate lines of wires, poles, tunnels, conduits and other works In the manner and to the extent required for the corporate purposes of the company, and to conduct, store, sell and supply electricity and other power and with such lines of wire, poles, conduits, motors or other conductors or devices to conduct, convey, furnish or receive such electricity to or

column1: from any person at any place, through, over, along or across any publie highway, bridges, viaducts, railways, water courses, or over or under any waters, etc., and

column2: To erect poles, construct trenches or conduits or do other things necessary for the transmission of heat or light as fully as the circumstances of the case may require, provided the same are so constructed as not to incommode the public use of streets, highways or public places, or to impede the access to any house or other building erected in the vicinity thereof, or to interrupt the navigation of any waters, the company, however, being responsible for all damages which it causes in carrying out or maintaining any of its works.

column1: The powers of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company including those above mentioned, may be exercised without the consent of any municipal corporation, the right of the company to so exercise them having been, as we are advised, affirmed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council In the case of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company v. Corporation of the Town of North Toronto, 1912, A.C. page 834.

We have been apprised that your Committee is now considering Bill No. 13, an Act to consolidate and amend the Railway Act, certain provisions of which, if enacted in the form in which they appear in the copy of the Bill which we have seen, would seriously limit and impair the rights, powers and privileges of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, and would correspondingly affect the security for the bonds of The Electrical Development Company of Ontario, Limited.

It is, of course, obvious that the value of the undertaking of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company depends wholly on its ability to market the power which it transmits from Niagara over its transmission lines, and an impairment of its ability to effect such distribution would, therefore, result in serious loss to the holders of the bonds of the Electrical Development Company.

As trustees for the bondholders of the Electrical Development Company of Ontario, Limited, under the circumstances above set out, we beg respectfully to submit that the provisions of the draft Act to consolidate and amend the Railway Act, above referred to, should be so amended as not to impair or limit the charter rights of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, or that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, should be excepted from their operation, so long as any of the bonds of the Electrical Development Company of Ontario, Limited, remain outstanding.
Tours faithfully,
Trust Officer^

I have no brief to act for any of these parties. I never had any consultation with any of them. I never heard anything in connection with this question except what I heard publicly before the committee. My objection is that we are confiscating a right to which this company is legally entitled. I am surprised that the minister is making such a proposal to the House. I have great faith in his fairness, and I was able to agree with him on nearly everything in connection with this Railway

Act white we were considering it, excepting this one thing. I cannot make up my mind to agree to the course pursued by the minister in regard to this matter, and I want to put myself on record as opposed to it, and to vote against it.

The minister has briefly outlined the situation, but it must not be forgotten that in Ontario, under a Provincial Act, there has been undertaken a work that has not been undertaken elsewhere. The Hydro-Electric Commission, acting by virtue of a statute of Ontario, has undertaken and put in force what is without doubt the greatest public work of this kind anywhere in the world, controlled by the province and by the municipalities. It can be understood that in connection with such a scheme as that difficulties will be met with in the way of vested rights held by companies, and it must not be forgotten that privileges granted to companies by this Parliament and by the Legislature of Ontario previously, never contemplated the situation that has arisen; and, in justification of this amendment and of some very drastic legislation, perhaps in some instances too drastic, passed 'by the Ontario Legislature, it must be remembered that the object of all this was to remove obstacles from the way of the full development of the Hydro-Electric system, in a large measure that accounts for this amendment, although the explanation may be a little intricate and might not be of interest to this House. column1: The board holds an investigation and makes an order which is binding on the company and on the municipality. That is

Mr. A. 0. MACDONELL: My hon. friend is also my learned friend and we both understand Cjourt proceedings and I would prefer to proceed. As offsetting the Railway Act the company set up the charter it had.

This is the only company that still possesses its. original wide power of going everywhere or anywhere without license. A number of power companies have been incorporated by the Dominion Parliament, and they have come here from time to time-I am talking now within the knowledge of members of this committee-to get amendments

to their charters in various ways, extending their powers, adding to their borrowing powers, adding to their capital and so on. And in every case where they have come here, they have been saddled with these public-safeguarding clauses, because many of these charters are old charters. During this present session the Continental Light, Heat and Power Company of Montreal, which was I think incorporated in' 1897, came hare and was saddled with half a dozen of these public-safeguarding clauses. They had a 'charter very similar to this charter. Since this Toronto and Niagara Power Company never came here to get an amendment, there .has been no opportunity to .amend its charter by adding the safeguarding clauses, anad therefore it became essential that some provision be made in some way to restrict these wide powers. The company was not satisfied to be bound by the general Railway Act of Canada, as interpreted by the Court of Appeal of the province of Ontario, and, as I said, appealed to the Privy Council. The case is reported in the Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1912, at page 834. In this case the Privy Council reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals of Ontario, and held that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company was not bound by the general Railway Act, and that it did not need the consent of a municipality to go anywhere, that it was absolutely at large to go where it pleased, without leave or license, under the special Act of 1902. Does any member of this committee agree that that .is a safe or fair thing to permit, that a power company should have the right to go anywhere in Canada in any street, highway, square or public place, cross it, to do as it pleases, without any consent, and to set up in that community [DOT]as a distributing company selling power? In this case the Toronto and Niagara Power Company were the plaintiffs, and the corporation of the town of North Toronto, defendant, on appeal from the Court of Appeals for Ontario. The head note is as fol- [DOT] lows:
Held that by sections 12 and 13 of their incorporating Dominion Act, II Edward VII, chapter 107-
That is the Toronto and Niagara Power Company incorporating Dominion Act.
-the appellants-
That is the Toronto and Niagara Power Company.
[DOT]-were empowered to enter upon the streets of North Toronto without the consent of its municipal council for the purpose of erecting poles to carry power lines for the conveyance of electricity.
Held, further, that section 90 of the Railway Act of 1888 as amended by the Railway Act of 1899 and by section 247 of the Railway Act of 1906,-
That is the section I have read twice.
-the effect of which would be to give the respondents
That is the municipality.
-a veto upon the appellants' exercise of their powers, is inconsistent with the said sections 12 and 13 of the .special Act, and consequently by section 21 thereof-
That is the power company Act.

-is rendered inapplicable to the appellants; section 247, moreover, applies only to companies within the definition clause of the Act of 1906, that is, railway companies; while subsections 3 and 4 thereof save the appellants' powers under their special Act.

What the Privy Council decided was this, that although our Railway Act is burdened with definitions of a company and what constitutes a company coming under the Act and being subject to the Act, a power company, according to the Privy Council, does not come under the Railway Act. The Privy Council held that, inasmuch as this was not a railway company, it was not bound by the word ""company"" as defined by_ the Railway Act, that the Railway Act, in so far as power companies were concerned, only referred to or related to railway companies that were selling or distributing power, and did not have any reference to the general power companies, and this I submit is entirely contrary to the spirit and intention of the legislation. Let me read a paragraph from Lord Haldane's judgment on that point, in which he admits that the intention apparently was that all these companies should be included under the term ""railway company,"" and that a railway company in the definition of ""company"" included these companies, yet the strict meaning of the Act, according to the Privy Council, excluded a power company from the operation of the Act, and the power companies were not bound by the Act at all. Lord Haldane said:
The Parliament of Canada, not unnaturally, anxious to avoid dangers of this kind,-
That is the kind of conflict that arose in this case.

-accordingly passed general statutes conferring upon the municipal authorities large powers of control. Section 90 of the Railway Act 1888, was amended by the Railway Act of 1899, which added to it a subsection illustrative of this kind of control.
This is important. The Railway Act of 1899 was afterwards embodied into the Act of 1906.

The new subsection enacted that when any company had power by any Act of the Parliament of Canada to construct and maintain lines of telegraph or telephone or for the conveyance of light, heat, power, or electricity, such company might, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon for the purpose of exercising such power. ... If the powers conferred by this section displaced the less restricted powers of entering without any consent conferred by the Act of incorporation the appellants are in the wrong.
That is the power in the special Act.

Their Lordships have, therefore, to determine this question. They have to bear in mind that a Court of justice is not entitled to speculate as to which of two conflicting policies was intended to prevail, but must confine itself to the construction of the language of the relevant Statutes read as a whole.

Now, under that reading, they excluded the intention which Lord Haldane recites was the spirit and foundation for the section of the Railway Act which I have read, but he says he must construe it literally, and the court construed it literally according to their interpretation, and the effect of that was that the appeal was dismissed and the Toronto and Niagara Power Company was left absolutely at large.

That is, it is free to go where it pleased, without leave or license. It is not bound by the Railway Act, according to the judgment of the Privy Council. It is not bound by any of the safeguards of the Railway Act. It has never come to Parliament for a moment, so that it can be reached and safeguarding provisions enacted, and there it is to-day. The only way of reaching it is by 'the provision made in this legislation. As I have said, this legislation was asked for by the united municipalities of Canada, not only Ontario, but outside of Ontario, by the Ontario Government, and by various other municipalities and communities, including the Hydro-Electric Power Commission, because, unless this clause is enacted this company can invade any place without anybody's consent, or leave or license. The necessity for making the section retroactive was this: this power company is not selling retail power; it is a producer of power.

Provided that this subsection shall not prevent the company from delivering or supply, ing such power by any means now existing or under the provisions of any contract now in force for use in the operation of any railway or for use by any other company lawfully engaged in the distribution of such power within any such city, town, village or township.

column1: does not hurt anybody to begin with. It is a precaution. I am a member of the committee and I am not advocating anything special except that I want to see what the committee has done, by a vote of nine to three, goes through the House. This clause was explained at length and questions were asked, and it was proved, to the satisfaction of the committee that the Toronto Electric Light Company, and the Toronto-Niagara Power Company, and a number of other kindred companies, are practically an association of companies under one aegis or management, or whatever you like to call it. I do not ask hon. members to take my word for this; it is contained in the memoranda submitted to this House by the Government of Ontario, which was sent to the chairman of the committee and read by him. There was only one arrangement. The Toronto Electric Light Company had a contract with the city of Toronto, which expires in two or three years, and what is apprehended, and it was alleged before the committee, and the statement was actually made, that the Toronto Electric Company, which has an expiring and perishable franchise, expiring in two or three years or thereabouts, will, it is expected, turn over to the Toronto-Niagara Power Company all its business, poles, plant, machinery and equipment, and then the Toronto-Niagara Power Company can continue ad- infinitum to operate the Toronto Electric Light Company the same as if there had been no contract between the Toronto Electric Light Company and the city of Toronto, and this retroactive clause is inserted to prevent that improper act. It hurts nobody. It is an insurance, a precaution, and a public safe-

guard. The same thing might happen in other communities. The Toronto-Niagara Power Company may go elsewhere and purchase electric light or power companies that have perishable and expiring franchises and then the business will pass over to the company with a permanent franchise forever. I have tried to make myself understood; I do not know whether I have done so or not, and I appeal to the fairness of the committee to pass this legislation to protect municipal rights, to protect municipalities and the public. The people came here from all over Ontario and from some parts of Quebec to ask that this be done, and there is nothing wrong in it. It is a safeguard. We are not saddling this company with any more safeguards than any other company is saddled with, but we ask that this clause be retained, for the purpose of carrying out the wishes of the people to whom I have referred, who came here with their counsel, and argued the matter at very great length, and answered every question put to them by the members of the committee. No matter was more fully or fairly dealt with by that select committee, and I appeal to this committee to carry out what was done by that committee, and to pass the section as framed.
