My hon. friend has spent half an hour arguing before the committee, as though we were the Supreme Court, showing us what the Privy Council decided, and he said that unless something was done, the company had power to extend its lines as it liked, into Toronto or any other municipality. That is true. But my hon. friend forgot to tell the committee the law on which the Privy Council made its decision. My hon. friend knows it all right, but I want to give it to the other members of the committee. I refer to section 247 of the Railway Act of 1906, which reads as follows:
When any company is empowered by special Act of the Parliament of Canada to construct, operate and maintain lines of tele-

graph or telephone, or for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, the company may, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, etc.

Then it provides that they can do certain things, and here are the conditions. First, there shall be accessibility of traffic to the public, then a provision that the wires shall be not less than 22 feet above the ground. No trees shall be cut down unless it is necessary. Then it is provided that the opening of any street, square or other place for the erection of poles or for the carrying of wires shall be subject to the supervision of such person as the municipal council may appoint, and there shall be temporary removal of wires, and all that sort of thing. All these things are when the company is authorized to do certain things under a special Act. Subsection 8 provides:

Nothing contained In this section shall be deemed to authorize the company to exercise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages without the company having first obtained consent therefor by a by-law of the municipality.

But unfortunately the special Act incorporating- the company did authorize them to distribute, and the Privy Council held, and rightly, I believe, that as this section 247 refers to special Acts, and as the special Act of this company gave it the actual power to distribute, they had a right to distribute it. That is the law. I want to call attention to the fact that the gentleman who prepared this Bill, Mr. Price, was not before the committee. Evidently he is a lawyer of distinction, because he has put in our hands a memorandum showing the legal effect of every amendment or change that was made in the Railway Act. When Mr. Price drafted this section he included telegraph, telephone and power companies all in one section. The subcommittee, I think for the purposes of my hon. friends from Toronto, divided it up and put telegraph and telephone companies in one section and electric light and power companies in another. Mr. Price says:

The provisions of this present section requiring telegraph, telephone and power companies within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada to get consent of the municipality or leave of the Board before putting their wires upon, along or across any highway or public place will apply notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any Special Act or in any other Act and notwithstanding any power or authority conferred by or under any Act.

My hon. friend has spent half an hour setting forth the decision of the Privy Council under a special law referring only to the special Act of this company. But subsection 2 of section 374, as presented to this committee, is as follows:-

Notwithstanding anything contained in any special or other act or authority of the Parliament of Canada or of the legislature of any province, the company shall not, except as in this section provided, acquire, construct, maintain or operate any works, machinery, plant, line, pole, tunnel, conduit or other device upon, along, across, or under any highway, square or other public place within the limits of any city, town, village or township, without the consent of the municipality. ^

Mr. Price absolutely met all the conditions of the Privy Council case. He provided that notwithstanding anything in the special Act a company may not erect a pole, line, or conduit, whether for distribution or transmission-

Putting lines and wires upon highways and public places. Here an important change is made. string a wire, either for transmission or distribution, without the consent of the municipality. My hon. friend draws a distinction between transmission and distribution, but that is only a technical point. Usually a line which has high voltage is called a transmission line; when the voltage is somewhat reduced, it is called a distribution line. However, under the provision as drafted by Mr. Price, a company may not erect a line, pole, or anything that carries electricity, in any municipality without the consent of the municipality. And, if the municipality is unfair, the right of . appeal to the Railway Board is provided, and it is for the Railway Board to set out the conditions under which this distribution and transmission shall take place.

This Parliament is the only body having power to remedy that condition, and Mr. Price drafted this section of the Railway Bill with a view to remedying it. But my hon. friends from Toronto are not satisfied that matters of this kind should, in case of dispute, be left to the Railway Board. Notwithstanding the fact that in every other like case the matter is referred to the Railway Board they want it differently in Toronto. Therefore they pult in two extra clauses, declaring what the law should have been ten years ago and absolutely preventing the companies concerned from going to the Railway Board. They take it out of the power of this company to extend its lines except with the consent of the city of Toronto^-and they know that the company cannot get that consent. Knowing that, they re-

fuse that, appeal to the Railway Board which may be had in all other cases. In no case that came up during the whole discussion of this Bill did I not say: leave it to the Railway Board. I gave my vote on numerous occasions, and in those cases* where the matter, did not come to a vote,
I gave it as my opinion:
column2: leave this to

column1: the Railway Board.
I believe the Railway Board is one of the finest institutions in the British Empire.

I think they are trying to work out the railway law of Canada on just as good lines as they possibly can. I have such faith in them that no matter what railway matter comes up I would say, leave it to the board.

I say so to-night. If a question comes up between the Electric Light Company and' the city of Toronto, I would say, 'leave it to the board. There is no more reason why Toronto should not be governed by the general law any more than my little town of Woodstock, or any other town in this Dominion.

There is just one other observation I cannot refrain from making. My hon. friend says, ""If you don't put in these retroactive clauses the company may go to some other town and buy a plant there and give the people electric light."" What a crime that would be! Think of allowing any company to go to another city and supply people with light at competitive rates. Why in Montreal they are fighting rings around one another just to get competition; it is the very thing they want. Down in our country those gentlemen who have been unfortunate enough to invest their money in electric light are in constant fear that the municipalities will come into competition with them. But in Ontario, for Heaven's sake keep away from competition ! If you don't put in these retroactive clauses these men will go to some other town and give the people cheaper light than the Hydro Electric. What a crime that would be! I only need to refer to these matters to show the absolute unfairness of the whole transaction.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Donald Sutherland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7&Language=E&Section=ALL

No horses, sheep, swine, or other cattle shall be permitted to be at large upon any highway, within half a mile of the intersecton of such highway, with any railway at rail level, unless they are in charge of some competent person or persons, to prevent their loitering or stopping on such highway at such intersection, or straying upon the railway.
Subsection 3 says:

If the horses, sheep, swine, or other cattle, of any person which are at large contrary to the provisions of this section are killed by any train at such point of intersection, he shall not have any right of action against any company in respect of the same being so killed or injured.
Subsection 4 provided:

When any horse's, sheep, swine, or other cattle at large, whether upon the highway or not, get upon the property of the company and are killed or injured by a train, the owner of any such animal so killed or injured, shall, except in the eases otherwise provided for by the next following section, be entitled to recover the amount of such loss or injury against the company in any action in any court of competent jurisdiction, unless the company establishes that such animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act or omission of the owner or his agent, or of the custodian of such animal or his agent.

Section 295 provides that no person whose horses, cattle, or other animals are killed or injured by any train shall have any right of action against any company in respect of such horses, cattle, or other animals being so killed or injured, if the same were so killed or injured because of any person leaving the gates open.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL

and convenience of every member, but to my knowledge these gentlemen have gone away, having, as I say, received no intimation whatever that this Bill was coming up. It would be only fair, therefore, to put off the vote, if there is one, until after eight o'clock.

479620,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.17.1.2,1917-07-18,d37caeac-e2c8-4010-a406-bd6c910d1265,ca.m.6702,Mr. GRAHAM:,,"MILITARY SERVICE ACT, 1917.",CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.,,"I protest again. It is

absolutely unfair, and as far as I am concerned I shall take no part in the discussion. I have supported this Bill at every stage and propose to support it, and I do not think I am entitled to treatment of this kind fr.om the Government.

,Liberal,,George Perry Graham,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d37caeac-e2c8-4010-a406-bd6c910d1265&Language=E&Section=ALL
479621,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.17.1.3,1917-07-18,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN:,Solicitor General of Canada,MILITARY SERVICE ACT, 1917.",CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.,,"I stated on behalf of the Government that I did not feel like pressing this over the protest of hon. gentleman opposite, but in view of the arrangement made by the whips I say that hon. gentlemen should undertake that no objection will be raised at the next sitting of the House on the technicality that we did not give notice of the third reading coming up. It could be no more than a technicality, because xthe Bill would have been reported the other evening but for the request made on 'behalf of the leader of the Opposition. The Bill has been reprinted, and is in the hands of the. hon. members of this House, and I do not think, it is asking too much to go on with it. However, we are ready to defer to the wishes of hon. gentlemen opposite, even in the face of an arrangement that has been made; I stated that plainly before the . Speaker left the Chair. But I think we should have an understanding clear and definite that we will not be held up at the next sitting of the House and asked to defer the third reading until next Tuesday. Surely that is not unreasonable.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL
479622,ca.proc.d.1917-07-18.17.1.4,1917-07-18,80f4de9d-1b1a-4db1-93cf-9cb7b9b63dd4,ca.m.9843,Mr. CARVELL:,,MILITARY SERVICE ACT, 1917.",CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.,,"I am in the same position as my hon. friend from South Renfrew. I have given the Government all possible assistance in the passage of this Bill. I had not the slightest intimation that it was coming up to-day. We went into committee on the Railway Bill at three o'clock, and I think the hon. member for South Renfrew and I have given the Government every possible assistance in getting it passed. There are no two members in this House, except the Minister of Railways and Canals and the hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) who have sat here so continuously since three o'clock as the hon. member for South Renfrew and myself, and in view of that, and our atti-
tude towards this Bill, I do not think it is fair to ask us to bind people who are not here.
Progress reported.
